name: Direct democracy
summary: Direct democracy holds that citizens should make laws and major decisions themselves, by assembly, referendum or initiative, rather than delegating that power to elected representatives. Its classic statement is Rousseau's claim that sovereignty cannot be represented and that a law the people has not ratified in person is void. Rousseau still lets a small elected body administer and thinks the model fits only small states, and modern writers describe direct votes as mostly a supplement within representative systems.
scope: Direct democracy as Britannica defines it: citizens themselves decide specific issues, by assembly, referendum or initiative, instead of delegating that power, on the normative base of popular sovereignty, freedom and political equality. Britannica names Rousseau as its outstanding theorist, so his Social Contract (the case that sovereignty cannot be represented, laws need the people's own ratification) is read for the ideology's institutional tenets, and the Stanford Encyclopedia's account of his view of representation and government is read alongside it. The ideology is a view about who decides; it holds no stated positions on economics, culture, foreign policy or most social questions, so those statements are null. Rousseau's wider views (his economic equality, civil religion, penal doctrine) are not taken as the ideology's, and nor are modern practices such as Swiss votes or Athenian assemblies. Representative democracy is a separate subject.

sources.title: Direct democracy

sources.usedFor: Definition (citizens decide specific issues themselves rather than delegating), forms (assemblies, referenda, initiatives, recall), normative basis (popular sovereignty, freedom, political equality; Rousseau as the outstanding theorist), history and controversies.

sources.title: The Social Contract (full text, trans. G.D.H. Cole), in The Social Contract & Discourses (Project Gutenberg #46333)
sources.author: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
sources.usedFor: Sovereignty inalienable, indivisible and not representable; laws void unless ratified by the people; assemblies; majority rule; government as the people's officers; hereditary rule; election and lot.

sources.title: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
sources.author: New World Encyclopedia
sources.usedFor: Names Rousseau's argument for direct democracy over representative democracy and his book The Social Contract; ties the Social Contract text to the ideology.

clerical-rule.rationale: Britannica places direct democracy on popular sovereignty, and Rousseau says legitimate authority rests on convention among citizens, not on a priestly or divine claim (I.4, III.6).

confederal-coordination.rationale: Rousseau says deputies are mere stewards who can carry through no definitive acts, and for larger states he offers confederations of small self-governing units (III.15 and note).

consent-of-governed.rationale: Rousseau holds that conventions are the only basis of legitimate authority and that no one can be made subject without consent (I.4, IV.2); Britannica names popular sovereignty and freedom as the normative base.

decide-locally.rationale: Rousseau says the sovereign can act only when the people is assembled in person, so he wants states small and rejects uniting several towns under one capital (III.13, III.15).

democracy-is-procedure.rationale: Rousseau says a people that only elects representatives is free just at election time and that a law it has not itself ratified is void, so elections alone do not make a government democratic (III.15).

direct-votes.rationale: Britannica defines direct democracy by citizens deciding specific issues themselves through votes, and Rousseau holds that every law the people has not ratified in person is void.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Rousseau states that no man has natural authority over another and that conventions form the basis of all legitimate authority, and he dismisses the claim that God sends kings as a matter for the pulpit (I.4, III.6).

dynastic-succession.rationale: Rousseau argues that hereditary succession risks rulers who are children or fools (III.6), yet says a people may set up a hereditary government provisionally as its own decision (III.18).

experts-over-public.rationale: Britannica says that in direct democracy citizens act as decision makers instead of delegating, and Rousseau holds that a law the people has not ratified is void; he still lets an elected few administer.

generational-constitutional-review.rationale: Rousseau wants periodic assemblies that cannot be suppressed and always put the question whether the people wishes to keep the present form of government, since no fundamental law is irrevocable (III.18).

minority-veto.rationale: Rousseau holds that apart from the founding compact the vote of the majority binds all the rest, including those who voted against (IV.2).

one-party-rule.rationale: Rousseau holds that the people as a whole is sovereign and that no partial society should hold sway within the state, which excludes any one party's exclusive right to lead (II.3, III.14).

organic-representation.rationale: Rousseau holds that sovereignty cannot be represented and that no partial society should stand between citizen and state, so organised groups cannot replace parties as the basis of representation (II.3, III.15).

parliament-supreme.rationale: Rousseau says the English people are free only while electing members of parliament and that any law the people has not ratified in person is void, so no parliament is the supreme lawmaker (III.15).

participatory-democracy.rationale: Britannica says the normative case for direct democracy rests on the participatory theory of democracy, and Rousseau holds that in a free country citizens do public business in person.

people-in-arms.rationale: Rousseau says citizens of a free country do everything with their own arms and that hiring troops and staying at home leads to soldiers who enslave the country (III.15).

political-decisions-consensus.rationale: Rousseau says near-unanimity marks a healthy state and weighty questions should approach it, yet he holds that the majority vote binds all the rest (IV.1, IV.2).

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Britannica notes that representative elites developed a strong interest in monopolising power, and Rousseau says citizens who pay deputies to stand in end up with representatives who sell their country (III.15).

property-franchise.rationale: Rousseau calls the right to vote in every act of sovereignty one that no one can take from the citizens, and he wants no citizen too poor to be forced to sell himself (IV.1, II.11).

recall-officials.rationale: Rousseau says the officers who exercise executive power are not the people's masters and that the people can set them up and pull them down whenever it likes (Social Contract III.18).

recallable-delegates.rationale: For Rousseau deputies are only the people's stewards, and the people can dismiss those who administer government whenever it likes (III.15, III.18).

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Rousseau says that when government usurps sovereignty the compact is broken and citizens are forced but no longer bound to obey (III.10).

separated-powers.rationale: Rousseau separates legislative from executive power and calls assemblies the curb on government (III.1, III.14), yet declares sovereignty indivisible and mocks theorists who divide it (II.2).

single-common-good.rationale: Rousseau holds that only the general will, which looks to the common interest alone, may direct the state, and that the will of all, a sum of particular interests and partial associations, is not it (II.1, II.3).

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Rousseau says those who hold executive power are the people's officers owing obedience, and one who sets himself above the laws is a usurper and despot (III.10, III.18).

vote-delegation.rationale: The Stanford Encyclopedia says Rousseau treats handing one's right of self-rule to another as a form of slavery, and Britannica's defining mark is that citizens decide rather than delegate.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Rousseau says that when a citizen says of public affairs 'what does it matter to me' the state is lost, and that in a well-ordered city every man flies to the assemblies (III.15).

missingStatements.text: Voters should be able to remove elected officials from office before their term ends.
missingStatements.rationale: Recall is listed among the core mechanisms of direct democracy as a way for citizens to keep control over those they elect.

missingStatements.text: Citizens should be able to put a proposed law to a public vote by collecting signatures.
missingStatements.rationale: The citizens' initiative is a defining tool of direct democracy, as in Switzerland.

notes: Themes searched: government (representation, recall, lot, majority and unanimity, hereditary and elective rule, parties, separation of powers), liberty and means in Britannica, the Stanford Encyclopedia entries on Rousseau and on democracy, and Rousseau's full Social Contract; economic, cultural, ecological, technological, world and most social statements are outside what these sources state and are null. Rousseau himself favoured an elective aristocracy for administration and a very small state, so scholars dispute how fully democratic he was; modern advocates mostly accept hybrid, semi-direct systems. Participatory-democracy theorists (Pateman, Cole, Mill) are named by Wikipedia only and no defining source for them was opened, so they are not used. Britannica's account of Switzerland and the United States describes practice in states that are not run on this doctrine and is not used for answers.
